title: Understanding Interest and APR
summary: Compare the same borrowing need under different payments, rates, charges and timelines.
subtitle: A Tiny Monthly Payment Walks Into a Loan Ad. The Total Cost Waits Outside in Smaller Font.

blocks.text: Interest is the price paid for using borrowed money.

The interest rate helps work out that price. The annual percentage rate, or APR, shows the cost of borrowing as a yearly rate. Total repayment shows the dollars that leave your budget if the agreement runs as planned. These numbers work together, but they answer different questions.

In this Interest Decoder Lab, you will compare the same borrowing need under different payments, rates, charges and timelines. The lab motto is simple: numbers expose marketing. You do not need advanced math, only the patience to put every offer under the same light.
FCAC: Personal loans — know your rights
The monthly payment is a cash-flow question. Total repayment is a price question. A responsible decision must answer both.
The Six Numbers on the Decoder

items.title: PRINCIPAL
items.text: The amount you borrow or still owe, before interest and fees.

items.title: INTEREST RATE
items.text: The yearly rate used to work out interest on the balance.

items.title: APR
items.text: The yearly cost of borrowing, shown for comparison. It can differ from the interest rate when required charges are included.

items.title: PAYMENT
items.text: The amount due each payment period.

items.title: TIMELINE
items.text: How often you pay, how many payments there are and how long it takes.

items.title: TOTAL REPAYMENT
items.text: All scheduled payments and charges, under the stated assumptions.

items.title: “The lowest monthly payment is automatically the cheapest loan.”
items.text: A payment can be lowered by stretching out the repayment period. That may help monthly cash flow while raising the total you pay. Compare affordability and total cost together.

blocks.text: A $132-a-month difference can hide a $960 gap, and Lab Test 1 catches it before you sign.
blocks.detail: Three offers for the exact same amount are about to reveal which one is the deal, and which one just looks like it.
blocks.extra: Three loan offers get tested against the same $2,000 next.

sections.title: Lab Test 1: Hold the Borrowing Amount Still

blocks.text: For this made-up first test, each offer gives you the same $2,000 and has no extra required charge.
Multiply the payment by the number of payments to get the scheduled total. Subtract the $2,000 you received to get the borrowing cost in dollars.
Compare three offers
blocks.extra: Enter the amount borrowed, then each offer’s payment and number of payments. Watch the borrowing cost update.

items.title: OFFER A — $185 × 12 = $2,220
items.text: Borrowing cost: $220 — Can Owen safely carry $185 each month?

items.title: OFFER B — $75 × 36 = $2,700
items.text: Borrowing cost: $700 — Is the extra $480 versus A worth the lower payment?

items.title: OFFER C — $53 × 60 = $3,180
items.text: Borrowing cost: $1,180 — Does $22 less than B justify $480 more and two extra years?

blocks.text: THE DECODER SAYS
Offer C is $132 per month lower than A, but costs $960 more and lasts 48 months longer.
Offer B costs $480 less than C and ends 24 months earlier.
A smaller payment may mean a longer relationship with the debt. Count payments before admiring one payment.

items.title: A smaller payment can mean a longer debt.
items.text: A smaller payment can mean a longer debt.

items.title: Count every payment and compare total repayment.
items.text: Count every payment and compare total repayment.

items.title: “If the payment fits, the loan fits.”
items.text: A payment may fit this month and still be poor value or too shaky for the full term. Test it against irregular expenses, rate changes and the number of months it must last.

blocks.text: Meet Owen
paragraphs: Owen lives in Fredericton and needs a $2,000 laptop for contract work. Three offers promise payments of $185, $75 and $53. The $53 offer practically arrives carrying balloons. Owen pauses the celebration and reads the written terms. A payment can be charming without being cheap.

Owen first circles Offer C. Fifty-three dollars fits easily under his $90 monthly limit, and Offer A does not. Then he counts all 60 payments. The laptop might retire before the loan does, which is not the loyalty program he had in mind.

The salesperson says the $53 offer ends today and repeats the monthly amount four times. Owen asks for the amount borrowed, APR, number of payments, required charges and total cost in writing. Urgency can shorten a promotion. It should not shorten the comparison.

Owen gets the disclosure for all three offers and checks the same $2,000, monthly schedule and required charges. Offer A has the lowest total, but it is over his safe monthly limit. Offer B stays inside the limit and saves $480 and two years compared with C. The middle option is suddenly much less middle-of-the-road.

Owen’s safe limit is $90 a month, so he passes on Offer A even though it has the lowest total. He chooses Offer B at $75 and writes down the $2,700 total. He also sets a date to ask about extra payments. By skipping Offer C, he keeps $480 and finishes 24 months sooner. The best deal was the cheapest one he could carry every month, and that was not the tiniest payment. Offer C keeps its balloons. Owen keeps his $480.

blocks.text: Owen's decoder sheet turned three confusing offers into one clear, defensible choice.
blocks.detail: Splitting rate, APR and total repayment into separate jobs is what let Owen catch the $960 gap before it caught him.
blocks.extra: Lab Test 2 gives each number on your own offers a single job.

sections.title: Lab Test 2: Give Each Number One Job

items.title: LAYER 1 — INTEREST RATE
items.text: Use it to see how interest is worked out on the balance you owe. Confirm whether the rate is fixed or variable and how often interest is added.

items.title: LAYER 2 — APR
items.text: Use the disclosed APR for a fair comparison. Under federal rules, some required borrowing charges may be included and some left out, so read the fee list too.

items.title: LAYER 3 — TOTAL REPAYMENT
items.text: Use the disclosed total or the payment schedule to see the dollars paid over the full timeline. Confirm the assumptions, including term, payment frequency and any different final payment.

blocks.text: A Useful Estimate, and Its Limit
SIMPLE-INTEREST TRAINING ESTIMATE
$2,000 principal × 12% annual rate × 1 year = about $240 interest.
This is a basic estimate, not the calculation for every loan. Instalment loans may shrink the principal over time and add interest the way the agreement says.

Now add a required fee. Offer X has 10% interest and no required setup fee. Offer Y has 8% interest plus a required $150 borrowing charge. The lower interest rate does not settle the decision. Ask for the APR, payment schedule, amount received and total repayment.

items.title: “APR and interest rate are two names for the same number.”
items.text: They may match when interest is the only cost of borrowing. They can differ when required charges are part of the APR. Use the lender’s disclosure instead of trying to rebuild the APR yourself.

blocks.text: APR makes comparison fair. Total repayment turns the agreement into household dollars. Neither replaces the other.
Justice Laws: Financial Consumer Protection Framework Regulations

sections.title: Lab Test 3: Stress-Test the Rules Around the Rate

items.title: Fixed rate.
items.text: The stated rate stays the same for the agreed period, though the contract may still have fees or other conditions.

items.title: Variable rate.
items.text: The rate can move with a reference rate or formula in the agreement. Test whether your budget can handle an increase.

items.title: Payment frequency.
items.text: Weekly, biweekly and monthly payments are hard to compare until the number of payments and the timeline match.

items.title: Prepayment and missed-payment rules.
items.text: Confirm whether extra payments are allowed and what interest, fees or credit damage may follow a missed payment.

sections.title: Credit-Card Mini Lab: One Card, Different Interest Clocks

items.title: PURCHASE
items.text: At a federally regulated bank or credit union, purchases get a grace period of at least 21 days. To avoid purchase interest, pay the balance in full by the due date, as your agreement says.

items.title: CASH ADVANCE
items.text: There is no interest-free grace period. Interest generally starts on the day of the transaction, and the rate may be higher than the purchase rate.

items.title: BALANCE TRANSFER
items.text: A promotional rate may be temporary, and a transfer fee may apply. Confirm when interest begins, when the offer ends and what the rate is afterward.

blocks.text: FCAC: How credit cards work

items.title: “Every credit-card transaction gets the same grace period.”
items.text: Cash advances get no interest-free grace period, and balance transfers follow their own disclosed rules. The type of transaction can change the rate, the fee and the day interest begins.

blocks.text: The logo on the card stays the same. The interest clock may not. Label the transaction before calculating its cost.
Province Lens: Find the Right Rulebook

Federal banks and federal credit unions follow federal disclosure rules. Provincially regulated credit unions and lenders follow their province’s rules. This applies in Alberta, British Columbia, New Brunswick, Ontario, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland and Labrador. Check the lender, its regulator and your current agreement before relying on a rule or fee limit.

sections.title: Quick Check: What Must Be Compared?

items.title: Same principal, different payment count.
items.detail: Calculate total repayment and borrowing cost.

items.title: 8% plus a required fee versus 10% without it.
items.detail: Compare disclosed APR, charges and total repayment.

items.title: Variable rate.
items.detail: Test the payment and total if the rate rises.

items.title: Credit-card cash advance.
items.detail: Interest begins without an interest-free grace period.

items.title: Lowest total, unaffordable payment.
items.detail: Choose the lowest-cost option you can reliably afford, or delay borrowing.

blocks.text: Before You Compare Your Own Offers

items.title: “APR tells me everything I need to know.”
items.text: APR is useful, but it does not replace the payment amount, term, total repayment, rate type, optional products, extra-payment rules or what happens if you miss a payment. Compare the same borrowing need under the same assumptions.

blocks.text: A fair comparison keeps the amount, start date, payment frequency, repayment period and included charges consistent. Change one assumption at a time so you know what changed the answer.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Interest Decoder Sheet

blocks.text: Use two current written quotes and answer in your own words.
Do not record account numbers, passwords, card details, PINs, security answers or government ID numbers in course notes.
Interest Decoder Lab Closing Checklist

items.title: The borrowing need is fixed.
items.text: Offers are compared for the same amount and purpose, not whatever amount each seller prefers to quote.

items.title: The annual figures are separated.
items.text: Interest rate and APR are written down separately when the disclosure shows both.

items.title: The full timeline is counted.
items.text: Payment frequency, number of payments, term and any different final payment are all written down.

items.title: The dollar cost is known.
items.text: Total repayment and the amount received show the borrowing cost.

items.title: The decision survives a stress test.
items.text: Variable-rate, late-payment and uneven-income risks each have a written plan.

blocks.text: Decode borrowing by comparing the same need and separating interest rate from APR.
blocks.detail: Count every payment and charge, stress-test the contract and choose the lowest-cost option your household can reliably afford.

blocks.text: A good borrowing comparison asks “Smallest what: rate, payment, timeline or total cost?” and then answers all four.

items.title: Principal
items.text: The amount you borrowed or still owe, before interest and fees.

items.title: Interest
items.text: The price paid to a lender for using borrowed money.

items.title: Interest rate
items.text: The yearly rate used to work out interest on the balance.

items.title: APR
items.text: Annual percentage rate: the cost of borrowing shown as a yearly rate on the amount borrowed, under the disclosure rules that apply.

items.title: Fixed rate
items.text: A rate that stays the same for the agreed period.

items.title: Variable rate
items.text: A rate that may move with a reference rate or formula in the agreement.

items.title: Term
items.text: The period during which the credit agreement or current set of conditions applies.

items.title: Amortization period
items.text: The time needed to fully repay the loan on the planned schedule. It can be longer than the term.

items.title: Total repayment
items.text: The total dollars scheduled to be paid under the stated assumptions.

items.title: Grace period
items.text: A period when purchase interest may be avoided if the credit-card balance is paid as required. It does not apply to cash advances.
